by Mimi Billing

Good morning Luca,



Stockholm has been buzzing this week with the annual Tech Arena event, drawing around 12k attendees over two days.



Hosted in a vast arena usually reserved for soccer, ice hockey and concerts, the event featured partnership booths, coffee stations, three stages and dedicated areas for matchmaking, media and investors.



Tech Arena is often described as the Swedish answer to the Finnish tech conference Slush, but beyond the similarly dim lighting, it’s a very different affair. Despite strong stage appearances from Mistral’s Arthur Mensch, Lovable’s co-founder Fabian Hedin and Station F’s Roxanne Varza, plus a pitch competition, startups are only a small part of the program.



The event is just as much a platform for corporates and partners to showcase themselves. In honour of Zlatan Ibrahimović’s appearance, Vanta set up a soccer goal. Nordea handed out free ice cream, while Deutsche Telekom served a mix of German and Swedish fika.



As many tech event organisers know, it’s hard to keep scaleup founders on the conference floor. After their talks, Kry founder Johannes Schildt and Voi founder Fredrik Hjelm quickly disappeared, heading either back into the city or to the speakers’ lounge. Nor were many other high-profile founders lingering.



While VCs praised the dedicated investor day held ahead of the conference, some international VCs seemed underwhelmed by the scope of the main event. “Slush is much better,” one investor told me.



And yes, Slush is known to host a great gathering. But perhaps the ecosystem also needs events like this: spaces where politicians, corporates like Meta, banks, national organisations, service providers, investors, and startups all converge to “share ideas” — which appears to be the true focus here.



Last year, I felt Tech Arena lacked a clear identity. Now, I’m starting to think this breadth is its identity.



And personally, I appreciated drifting between the media zone, gossipy backstage conversations on big tech versus startups, and unexpected reunions with people I hadn’t seen in years.



Slush already exists. So why compete — when you can build something entirely different?

[https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6gIC!,w_40,c_scale,f_png,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack.com%2Ficon%2FLucideCheck%3Fv%3D4%26height%3D40%26fill%3Dtransparent%26stroke%3D%2523ea580c%26strokeWidth%3D3.6]Subscribed<https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9mdGF2LnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9hY2NvdW50IiwicCI6MTgwMTYwOTk2LCJzIjo2MTU2MTA1LCJmIjp0cnVlLCJ1Ijo0MjAyNzMwMSwiaWF0IjoxNzcwOTg4OTIwLCJleHAiOjIwODY1NjQ5MjAsImlzcyI6InB1Yi0wIiwic3ViIjoibGluay1yZWRpcmVjdCJ9.wNckCFMpr3-dTUn3OzviaSHf91BWjGQB9MwV1mxdTKk?>
The Gospel of the Immaculate Blockchain

Crypto, it’s often said, is a speed run of Finance 101<https://substack.com/redirect/383dcd98-6b0c-4f11-bc7f-1d570367542e?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. By creating from scratch an asset class that was insulated from reality, then making every mistake it was possible to make, crypto has been an expensive but mostly harmless way to teach finance from first principles.

It’s also said about bitcoin in particular that learning has been by devotional study. And fair enough, it’s a good story: from the annunciation by lowly mailing list<https://substack.com/redirect/3ce8fbe5-35c4-4d58-9e58-1be26592953d?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> to a conception most miraculous (an academic who didn’t want credit), plus numerous wise men<https://substack.com/redirect/1779e874-acee-49aa-8be2-01ae58763896?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> and an escape plan from a tyrannical establishment. Short of swaddling baby Satoshi in a tea towel and singing about cattle, the callback couldn’t be clearer.

But with bitcoin turning 18 years old in October, maybe it’s time to mark the end of the elementary phase and treat everyone involved as adults. Here’s something that happened this week<https://substack.com/redirect/0e602bec-230d-493d-ab9c-ce99d5741092?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>:

Susquehanna-backed crypto lender BlockFills has halted withdrawals and restricted trading on its platform, underscoring the strength of the recent tremors that have shaken the digital asset market.

The Chicago-based company, which in 2025 handled $60bn in trading volumes, has suspended client deposits and withdrawals as the price of bitcoin and other crypto assets has swung in recent days. The suspension was put in place last week but remains in effect, BlockFills told the FT.

The obvious echo is with 2022, when the gating of token shops started a domino effect that knocked over Three Arrows Capital, Celsius Network and FTX, among many others<https://substack.com/redirect/bdde4db6-7c0e-4cdb-b68d-234a798abe44?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Where it differs is the lack of amateur dramatics.

Crypto Winter was preceded by an altcoin sell-off and the bursting of the NFT bubble, both of which were widely anticipated, because altcoins and NFTs never seemed anything other than ridiculous. Bitcoin was insulated for a while thanks to demand from newly created ETFs<https://substack.com/redirect/d6c79bc2-7175-4847-8e1c-1cb1e605cd8f?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> and digital asset treasury companies<https://substack.com/redirect/6c86ea5c-1353-48a3-9d57-1dffbf0b2b9c?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, which people mistook for sensible money. It was only after the failure in May 2022 of TerraUSD, a stablecoin made of nonsense<https://substack.com/redirect/db38af7b-1323-4579-8045-cee77d65f5fb?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> and fraud<https://substack.com/redirect/c6fef4dc-55e8-4cbe-a567-242dea84c91a?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, that institutions began to question where all the tokens were.

This time round, with bitcoin nearly 50 per cent below its record high, we’ve skipped the preamble and gone straight to the action. Blockfills is a very grown-up sort of business, a CME-backed crypto intermediary that deals with clients who have at least $10mn in tokens. It’s not entirely expected for the first signs of distress to be at a broker for institutions and high-net-worth individuals.

The other big news in crypto this week involves Jeffrey Epstein, another broker of sorts for institutions and high-net-worth individuals. Recently released emails give weight<https://substack.com/redirect/44e3044c-d5d5-43eb-a428-9196af11ab0a?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> to the allegation that, in 2015, Epstein funded a team at MIT<https://substack.com/redirect/60c73d63-5a35-404a-aef4-147a939fb979?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> that steered bitcoin’s development away from internet money and turned it into a digital bearer bond.

Whether the involvement of a convicted paedophile tarnishes bitcoin’s Genesis story is a question for the faithful, so is none of our business. More measurable are the after-effects.

For the past decade or so, bitcoin has been marketed as digital gold. That’s awkward, firstly because bitcoin hasn’t been a store of value<https://substack.com/redirect/a621de6d-2aab-4eb4-a4a8-5b9a1b79a44a?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, but also because the gold market looks a lot like the kind of deflationary fiat money system bitcoin was proposed to fix. Goldsmiths invented fractional reserve banking in the 17th century by issuing loan notes, pretty much, and the value of paper gold in circulation dwarfs the trade in physical gold, which to a lot of people seems a bit suss<https://substack.com/redirect/a4acaec2-5a88-4b17-b66a-58a8b369cb44?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>.

But gold futures are contractual claims on gold, underwritten by 6,500 years of uncovered scams<https://substack.com/redirect/2bdba0c4-b662-4924-b5e5-3b84dcf15e46?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> and contested practices<https://substack.com/redirect/7e647dd5-7fe6-4d86-8696-0229c4e57c9e?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. The link between crypto futures and on-chain crypto can be more hazy. Neither side of a bitcoin perpetual futures contract ever needs to own a bitcoin, for example, any more than punters and bookmakers at the Kentucky Derby ever need to own a horse.

It’s hard to figure out how much of the $50bn or thereabouts of bitcoin futures open interest<https://substack.com/redirect/a3fa80e4-06b6-4aae-b0c0-e420a01db94e?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> has on-chain backing, but why assume it does? When a race has no finish line and is run via numbers on a screen, why involve horses at all?

We don’t know. BlockFills’ gating of funds may not turn out to be significant, but it’s still interesting. It suggests institutions aren’t waiting to find out where their tokens are. Below them are small-time gamblers with voided betting slips referencing tokens that may or may not exist<https://substack.com/redirect/9b0d2f97-2e8b-45af-b41b-2e518d922453?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. The big idea of bitcoin scarcity has been replaced by a crypto paper-printing machine whose fractional reserve can go all the way down to zero, and all the wise men left the scene a long time ago.

Rob Smith went in search of evidence for a subprime crisis conspiracy theory, debunked it, and replaced it with an even better conspiracy theory<https://substack.com/redirect/2ce8adf1-497e-44d4-b88c-a2d498ab37dd?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>.
